analysis.one_liner: Slaps a 25% tariff on Canadian lumber imports and rewrites trade-dispute appeal rules.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to put a 25% duty on Canadian lumber — 23 cosponsors split 11 Republicans and 12 Democrats — died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Emergency Lumber Act would have put a 25% tax on Canadian wood and lumber imports immediately, before any investigation had even decided whether Canada subsidized its lumber. It would have ordered a countervailing duty investigation into Canadian lumber, and directed the President to renegotiate NAFTA's Chapter 19 so Canadian firms could no longer appeal U.S. duties to binational panels — with U.S. courts, which rarely overturn trade decisions, taking over instead. If Canada and Mexico didn't agree within 150 days, the bill would simply end panel review by notice. The bill never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. lumber producers, who would sell more wood at higher prices behind a 25% tariff wall. The bill also helped them in a second, quieter way: NAFTA's Chapter 19 binational panels had been the arena where U.S. lumber duties were repeatedly challenged and often undone, and this bill would have taken those appeals away and replaced them with review in U.S. courts. A few members from wood-product districts would have had a vote to show their constituents.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an immediate 25% duty on Canadian wood and lumber products, effective 15 days after enactment, raising the price of imported Canadian lumber and letting U.S. producers charge more for their competing wood.

Orders the Commerce Department to open a countervailing duty (subsidy) investigation into Canadian lumber within 30 days, with the 25% duty staying in place until the investigation ends — a path to duties made permanent by an official finding.

Directs the President to renegotiate NAFTA and the U.S.-Canada Free-Trade Agreement so antidumping and countervailing duty decisions are reviewed by U.S. courts rather than the binational panels that trade rules currently require; if no agreement is reached within 150 days, the bill unilaterally ends panel review and moves pending appeals to the U.S. Court of International Trade.

analysis.who_pays: American homebuilders, homebuyers, and anyone who buys lumber, who would pay the 25% duty in the form of higher lumber and housing prices. Canadian lumber exporters would lose U.S. sales, and U.S. trading partners could be expected to treat the unilateral end of treaty-backed panel review as a breach of NAFTA and retaliate.

drawbacks.text: The 25% duty is a tax on imported lumber that lands on the people who buy it — raising construction costs and new-home prices — while the benefit flows to a single industry.

It imposes the penalty duty first and investigates later: a 25% duty would take effect just 15 days after enactment, before the required countervailing duty investigation had made any finding that Canada actually subsidized its lumber.

If Canada and Mexico did not agree to renegotiate within 150 days, the bill would end their treaty right to panel review by unilateral notice and strip it from merchandise already in the appeals pipeline, a step that trades the certainty of a negotiated trade agreement for a likely dispute and possible retaliation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are narrow and concentrated: a protected U.S. lumber industry earning more per board-foot. The costs are broad and diffuse: a 25% price increase on the main material in American homebuilding, a penalty imposed before any investigation had proven a subsidy, and a unilateral end to treaty-negotiated dispute review that invites retaliation against U.S. exports. An honest supporter would have to admit the bill protects one industry by taxing everyone who buys or builds a home.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee's trade subcommittee and then to a Rules subcommittee, and it sat there with no hearing and no vote until the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. James Longley of Maine and five original cosponsors introduced the bill on December 18, 1995, at the height of the U.S.-Canada softwood lumber fight.

The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Rules Committee the day it was introduced, then sent to the Trade Subcommittee on December 22, 1995 and to the Rules subcommittee on January 3, 1996.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed. The bill sat in subcommittee for the rest of the 104th Congress, which ended January 3, 1997, and the bill died there.

The broader policy fight over Canadian lumber did not end with the bill: the U.S. and Canada later negotiated the 1996 Softwood Lumber Agreement, which managed the trade with quotas and fees rather than the 25% duty this bill proposed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S. homebuilders and homebuyers, who were never charged a 25% tariff on lumber, and Canadian lumber exporters, who kept tariff-free access to the U.S. market. The bill's sponsors and supporters got nothing from it.

for.name: Rep. James B. Longley Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Emergency Lumber Act of 1995 on December 18, 1995.

for.name: 23 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: U.S. softwood lumber industry
for.role: Domestic lumber producers seeking protection from Canadian imports
for.what_they_did: Long ran a public campaign for countervailing duties against Canadian lumber and an end to Chapter 19 panel rulings against U.S. duties — the exact remedies this bill provided.

against.name: Phil Crane
against.role: Chair, Trade Subcommittee, House Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or vote after it was referred to the subcommittee on December 22, 1995.

against.name: Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The full committee took no action on the bill after referral; it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was genuinely bipartisan — 23 cosponsors split 11 Republicans and 12 Democrats — and since it never reached a vote, no party-bloc opposition ever appears in the record; the bill simply died quietly in committee.

industries.note: A 25% duty would let them raise prices behind a tariff wall, and eliminating NAFTA's Chapter 19 binational panels would remove the forum where U.S. lumber duties had been repeatedly challenged and overturned. Their gain comes directly out of homebuilders' and homebuyers' budgets.
Lumber is a core input to new homes; a 25% duty on imported Canadian lumber would raise framing costs and ultimately new-home prices for their customers.

The duty and the automatic subsidy investigation would raise their cost of selling into the U.S. market and could shut them out of it; their interest in defeating the bill ran alongside American consumers'.
